title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules, CI/CD and runbook
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Operational playbook and reference for managing Redwood's GPU fleet, related cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines for infra changes, and the on-call/runbook procedures for capacity incidents.
audience: Infra engineers, SREs, platform engineers, and on-call responders
scope: This document covers: GPU fleet capacity planning and sizing; cluster and node-pool conventions; cloud account and VPC networking standards for inference clusters; Terraform/IaC module references and recommended patterns; CI/CD and build pipelines for infra changes; and operational runbooks for capacity and networking incidents. It does not cover application-level model tuning or customer-specific private deployment procedures (see eng-private-deployments).
introduction: Purpose: Provide a single, actionable reference for infrastructure engineers who operate and evolve Redwood's GPU capacity and the supporting cloud networking and IaC. Goals: predictable capacity, safe change management, reproducible infrastructure, and rapid incident resolution while maintaining cost efficiency.
objectives:
- Maintain sufficient headroom to meet latency SLOs and throughput commitments for hosted and dedicated customers.
- Standardize IaC modules and CI/CD so infra changes are auditable and reversible.
- Define clear on-call runbooks and escalation paths for capacity, networking, and build failures.
- Document networking and cloud account patterns to minimize blast radius and ensure secure connectivity.
gpu-fleet-architecture:
Overview:
- Cluster types: inference-cluster (stable capacity for hosted API), burst-cluster (ephemeral burst capacity for autoscaling), dedicated-cluster-{customer} (tenant-isolated pools).
- Node pools: gpu-large (A100-40GB or equivalent), gpu-medium (A10G), gpu-small (T4/GV100 for dev and low-priority).
- Control plane: Redwood orchestration (kube-based scheduler + custom routing) manages pod placement and model variants.
- KV and prefix cache: colocated memcached/Redis clusters with network policies restricting access to inference clusters.
Design choices and rationale:
- Heterogeneous node pools simplify cost/performance tradeoffs and allow model pinning by instance type.
- Use taints/tolerations and node selectors to control scheduling for dedicated pools.
- Prefer vertical scaling of node counts over instance size changes to reduce kernel/CUDA variance during runtime.
capacity-planning-and-sla-targets:
Key metrics and targets:
- Latency SLOs: p95 <= 250ms for hosted text generation (short prompts), p50 for embeddings <= 30ms.
- Utilization targets: aim for 60-70% GPU utilization during steady state. >85% sustained triggers scaling or capacity add.
- Buffer policy: keep a 20% standby capacity for sudden spikes; additional 15% reserved for canary/rollouts.
- Autoscaling latency: target reaction time <= 60s for scale-up on sustained queue growth.
Sizing calculations (example):
- Workload: average token generation rate 500k tokens/min, average cost 0.002 GPU-seconds/token on A100-40GB.
- Convert to GPU seconds: 1,000 GPU-seconds/min required -> equivalent to 60k GPU-seconds/hour -> choose node count based on node GPU capacity.
Operational guidelines:
1. Weekly capacity review: review 7-day trend, 95th-percentile queue depth, and on-call incidents.
2. Quarterly capacity planning: add capacity for projected 20% growth or longer-term commitments.
3. Reserved vs spot mix: default production clusters use 70% reserved/commit + 30% spot for cost efficiency; dedicated clusters are 100% reserved.
node-pool-and-labeling-standards:
Naming and labels:
- Cluster name format: <env>-<purpose>-<region> (e.g., prod-inference-us-west-2).
- Node pool format: <nodepool>-<instance>-<priority> (e.g., gpu-large-a100-priority).
- Labels: role=inference | tier=hosted|dedicated|dev | gpu_type=a100|t4.
Terraform module references (names):
- modules/gke/gpu-node-pool
- modules/iam/gpu-node-pool-roles
- modules/monitoring/gpu-metrics-exporter
Conventions:
- Use immutable node pool upgrades: create new node pool, cordon/drain old nodes, delete after soak.
- Taint dedicated pools with dedicated=true:NoSchedule to prevent tenant bleed.
cloud-accounts-and-networking-standards:
Account model:
- Accounts per environment: production, staging, dev, sandbox.
- Dedicated customer accounts for Private deployments when required by compliance.
VPC and subnet conventions:
- Central VPC per region with per-cluster subnets: /20 for inference clusters, /24 for control-plane services.
- Private subnets for GPU nodes with NAT gateway for egress.
- Use AWS Transit Gateway / GCP Shared VPC where cross-account routing is needed.
- DNS and service discovery: internal DNS zone redwood.internal; use private hosted zones for account-specific names.
Security and firewall rules:
- Cluster security groups restrict ingress to API gateways and observability endpoints.
- Only control-plane bastion and CI runners allowed SSH access; all else via SSM Session Manager.
- KMS keys per-account for disk and S3 bucket encryption; access via IAM roles with least privilege.
terraform-and-iac-modules:
Module guidance:
- Keep modules small and focused: network, compute (node-pool), iam, monitoring, autoscaling, k8s-addons.
- Version pinning: every module must have a semver tag; consumers reference specific tag.
- Module repository structure: git repo "infra-modules" with directories: network/, compute/, iam/, monitoring/, k8s/.
- Example usage snippet (Terraform):

```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//compute/gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.4.2"
  cluster_name = "prod-inference-us-west-2"
  instance_type = "a100-40gb"
  node_count = 8
  labels = { role = "inference", tier = "hosted" }
  taints = [{ key = "dedicated", value = "false", effect = "NO_SCHEDULE" }]
}
```

Best practices:
- Use terraform workspaces or per-account state backends (S3/GCS with locking).
- CI should run terraform plan with the same var files as apply environment and require approvals for plans that change compute counts or networking.
ci-cd-and-build-pipeline:
Pipeline responsibilities:
- PR validation: linting, fmt, unit tests for modules (terratest), and a terraform plan.
- Canary apply: merge triggers apply to staging namespace; production requires manual approval.
- Change window: production node-pool scale-ups allowed 24/7; network topology changes require scheduled maintenance and two approvers.
Pipeline example steps:
1. PR opens: run tflint, fmt check, terratest unit tests.
2. On changes to modules/*: run integration terratest in ephemeral project.
3. Merge to main: pipeline runs terraform plan against staging account.
4. Apply to staging automatically.
5. Post-apply smoke tests: deploy small load test job to verify provisioning.
6. Promote to production: manual approval required; apply runs with `apply-lock` and notifies #infra-ops.
Rollback and drift detection:
- All applies generate a runbook entry with plan id and git sha.
- Schedule daily tfstate drift checks and alert on manual changes to critical resources (node counts, IGWs, TGWs).
observability-metrics-and-alerting:
Required metrics (exporters):
- GPU metrics: utilization, memory usage, temperature, encoder/decoder queue lengths.
- Pod-level metrics: request queue depth, p95 latency, token throughput, error rates.
- Node-level metrics: CPU, memory, disk, kernel errors, oom events.
Dashboards:
- Cluster overview: aggregate GPU utilization, free GPUs, average queue depth.
- Per-nodepool: utilization by model tag and customer.
Alert thresholds (examples):
- GPU free count < 10% for 5m -> P1 paged to oncall.
- Queue depth growth > 30% over 3m -> P1.
- Node provisioning failure rate > 5% for 10m -> P2 alert to infra channel.
Escalation: Pager duty -> infra oncall -> platform lead -> engineering manager if unresolved for 30m.
runbooks-and-incident-playbooks:
Runbook: High GPU saturation (P1)
1. Pager fires with alert id and cluster.
2. On-call: confirm alert on dashboards, check recent scale events and cluster autoscaler logs.
3. Immediate mitigation steps (ordered):
   a. Increase node pool target by +20% via Terraform emergency var override and apply (follow apply-lock).
   b. If spot interruptions causing loss, failover to reserved pool: trigger reserved scaling group increase.
   c. If autoscaler stuck: restart autoscaler deployment and verify IAM role/permissions.
4. After remediation: run a smoke test load to validate p95 latencies.
5. Post-incident: create incident report, update capacity forecasts, and propose pre-warming if repeatable.
Runbook: Networking - Cross-account connectivity failure (P2)
1. Check Transit Gateway/VPC peering status and route tables.
2. Verify Security Group and NACL changes in the change log.
3. If change identified, roll back via Terraform to previous state after approval.
4. If routing requires Emergency fix: update route table and coordinate with network lead for postmortem.
oncall-checklist-and-playbook:
Pre-shift checklist:
- Verify dashboards are loading and API keys are valid.
- Check pending PRs for infra changes scheduled in next 24h.
- Confirm capacity buffer >= 20% for production clusters.
During incident:
- Triage alerts within 5 minutes.
- Communicate in #infra-incidents with incident id and short summary.
- Use runbook steps; record each action in the incident timeline.
Post-incident:
- Complete postmortem within 72h and assign corrective actions.
- Update documentation and Terraform module tests if issue caused by infra code.
change-management-and-approvals:
Change types and approvals:
- Safe changes (labels, non-production scale): peer review + CI -> merge.
- High-risk changes (network, IAM, production node count/instance family): require two approvers including network/security owner and a manual gate in CI.
- Emergency changes: documented emergency approval flow with oncall + manager signoff post-hoc in the incident ticket.
Audit and tagging:
- All applies must include git sha and CI build id in a resource tag (tag:provisioned_by and tag:git_sha).
- Maintain an audit log in S3/GCS of terraform plans and apply outputs for 365 days.
backout-and-rollback-procedures:
Rollback patterns:
- Immutable resources: create replacement node-pool and migrate traffic back.
- Network changes: revert to previous Terraform state and re-apply after approvals.
- Use `terraform state` only as last resort; prefer plan-based revert.
Checklist before rollback:
1. Identify impact window and notify stakeholders.
2. Take backups (snapshot volumes, export config).
3. Execute rollback in staging first for identical change and smoke test.
4. Apply to production with approval and monitor metrics for 30m.
onboarding-and-runbook-for-new-models:
Pre-launch checklist for new model deployments:
- Model owners must supply: expected throughput, p95 latency target, memory footprint, preferred GPU type, and test payloads.
- Perf validation: run the benchmarking suite in a staging cluster and produce perf report (include token/sec and memory maps).
- IaC changes: add node-pool or labels if new GPU type required; create PR with terratest outputs.
- Traffic ramp: suggested rollout schedule: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows and rollback thresholds defined.
- Cost estimate: include expected monthly GPU-hour cost in PR description and signoff from finance for new heavy models.
